title: Ἀμφιμέδοντος λόγος
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Agamemnon’s soul asks Amphimedon what brought so many chosen men down to the dead, and recalls how he and Menelaus once came to Ithaca to win Odysseus over for the war against Troy. Amphimedon, speaking for the dead suitors, tells how it happened: Penelope’s web for Laertes, woven by day and unravelled by night for three years until a maid gave her away; the return of Odysseus in the guise of a beggar, with Telemachus; the contest of the bow; and the slaughter in the hall, where the suitors’ bodies still lie unburied. Agamemnon answers by praising Penelope’s faithfulness and the lasting song the gods will make for her, set against the infamy of his own wife. The scene then returns to the upper world, where Odysseus and those with him go down from the town to the farm of his father Laertes, where an old Sicel woman tends the old man.

sentences.t:
Ἀμφίμεδον, τί παθόντες ἐρεμνὴν γαῖαν ἔδυτε
πάντες κεκριμένοι καὶ ὁμήλικες;
sentences.tr:
Amphimedon, ti pathontes eremnēn gaian edyte
pantes kekrimenoi kai homēlikes;
sentences.l:
“Amphimedon, what having suffered did you enter the dusky earth,
all of you picked men and of one age?
sentences.i: “Amphimedon, what has happened to you, that you have all come down beneath the dusky earth, every one of you a picked man, and all of one age?
sentences.n: Agamemnon speaks to Amphimedon: Ἀμφίμεδον is the vocative. τί παθόντες is literally ‘having suffered what?’, the idiom for ‘what has happened to you, that …’. ἔδυτε is the aorist of δύω ‘enter, go down into’, and ἐρεμνήν is ‘dusky’, a different word from μέλας ‘dark’. κεκριμένοι is a perfect passive participle of κρίνω ‘separate, pick out’, so ‘picked men’, and ὁμήλικες is ‘of an age with one another’, put in the English as ‘of one age’ because no word follows for it to be ‘with’. The Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν ἄλλως
κρινάμενος λέξαιτο κατὰ πτόλιν ἄνδρας ἀρίστους.
sentences.tr:
oude ken allōs
krinamenos lexaito kata ptolin andras aristous.
sentences.l:
nor in any other way
choosing could one pick out the best men throughout the city.
sentences.i: Nor could a man, choosing in any other way, pick out the best men throughout the city.
sentences.n: κεν with the optative λέξαιτο makes a potential, ‘could pick out’, and the aorist middle participle κρινάμενος ‘choosing’ carries the condition (‘if he were choosing’), which the English gives as a participle. λέγω here is not ‘say’ but ‘gather, pick’. πτόλιν is the old form of πόλιν ‘city’, and ἄνδρας ἀρίστους is ‘the best men’. Agamemnon means that no selection made any other way could find better men than this company.

sentences.t:
ἦ ὔμμ’ ἐν νήεσσι Ποσειδάων ἐδάμασσεν,
ὄρσας ἀργαλέους ἀνέμους καὶ κύματα μακρά;
sentences.tr:
ē ymm’ en nēessi Poseidaōn edamassen,
orsas argaleous anemous kai kymata makra;
sentences.l:
Was it that you in the ships Poseidon subdued,
having roused grievous winds and long waves?
sentences.i: Was it Poseidon who overcame you in your ships, by rousing grievous winds and long waves?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question, ‘was it that …?’. ὔμμε is the epic accusative of ὑμεῖς ‘you’ (plural), and νήεσσι the dative plural of ναῦς ‘ship’. ἐδάμασσεν is the aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, and ὄρσας the aorist participle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. ἀργαλέους is ‘grievous’ and μακρά ‘long’, of waves. This is the first of two guesses about the cause of their death, a storm at sea; the Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.l:
Or perhaps hostile men harmed you on dry land,
cutting off cattle and the fine flocks of sheep,
or fighting for a city and for women?
sentences.i: Or did hostile men perhaps harm you on dry land, as you were driving off cattle and fine flocks of sheep, or fighting for a city and for women?
sentences.n: ἦ που ‘or perhaps’ opens the second guess, fighting on land. ἐδηλήσαντ’ is the aorist middle of δηλέομαι ‘harm’, and it has no object in the Greek: ‘you’ is understood from the first question, and the accusative participle περιταμνομένους agrees with it. μαχεούμενοι is nominative, so it cannot agree with that ‘you’: the Greek does not say whose fighting is meant. ἀνάρσιοι is ‘hostile’, and ἐπὶ χέρσου ‘on dry land’. περιταμνομένους is ‘cutting off’, a raider’s word for driving off a herd; πώεα is ‘flocks’, with οἰῶν ‘of sheep’. μαχεούμενοι is the epic form of μαχόμενοι, and πτόλιος the epic genitive of πτόλις.

sentences.t: εἰπέ μοι εἰρομένῳ·
sentences.tr: eipe moi eiromenōi·
sentences.l: Tell me, as I ask:
sentences.i: Tell me, now that I ask you:
sentences.n: εἰπέ is the aorist imperative of λέγω ‘tell’. μοι εἰρομένῳ is ‘to me as I ask’: εἰρομένῳ is the present participle of ἔρομαι ‘ask’, in the dative to agree with μοι. The ano teleia ends the unit and the reason for asking follows.

sentences.t: ξεῖνος δέ τοι εὔχομαι εἶναι.
sentences.tr: xeinos de toi euchomai einai.
sentences.l: And a guest-friend, to you, I declare myself to be.
sentences.i: I declare myself your guest-friend.
sentences.n: ξεῖνος here is the guest-friend, the man bound to another by the exchange of hospitality, not the plain ‘stranger’. εὔχομαι with an infinitive is ‘I declare (myself) to be’, the verb of a formal claim, and τοι is the dative ‘to you’. Agamemnon claims the bond from the visit that the next question recalls.

sentences.l:
Do you not remember when I came down there to your house,
to urge Odysseus, with godlike Menelaus,
to follow along to Ilios on well-benched ships?
sentences.i: Do you not remember when I came down to your house, to urge Odysseus, together with godlike Menelaus, to follow with us to Ilios on the well-benched ships?
sentences.n: ἦ οὐ opens a question that expects the answer ‘yes’. μέμνῃ is μέμνησαι, a perfect with present sense, ‘you remember’. κεῖσε is ‘thither, there’, and ὑμέτερον δῶ is ‘to your house’, δῶ being a short form of δῶμα. ὀτρυνέων is the epic future participle of ὀτρύνω ‘urge’, ‘meaning to urge’. ἅμ’ ἕπεσθαι is ‘to go along with (us)’. ἀντιθέῳ is ‘godlike’, and ἐϋσσέλμων νηῶν, with νηῶν the genitive plural of ναῦς, is ‘well-benched ships’.

sentences.t:
μηνὶ δ’ ἄρ’ οὔλῳ πάντα περήσαμεν εὐρέα πόντον,
σπουδῇ παρπεπιθόντες Ὀδυσσῆα πτολίπορθον.
sentences.tr:
mēni d’ ar’ oulōi panta perēsamen eurea ponton,
spoudēi parpepithontes Odyssēa ptoliporthon.
sentences.l:
And in a whole month we crossed all the broad open-sea,
with difficulty having persuaded the city-sacking Odysseus.”
sentences.i: We crossed all the broad sea in a whole month, having persuaded Odysseus, the city-sacker, only with difficulty.”
sentences.n: μηνὶ οὔλῳ is a dative of time, ‘in a whole month’: οὖλος is ‘whole’ in the traditional sense, though the word also means ‘thick, woolly’. πάντα agrees with πόντον, masculine accusative singular, so ‘all the broad sea’; περήσαμεν is the aorist of περάω ‘cross’. σπουδῇ is ‘with effort, with difficulty’. παρπεπιθόντες is the reduplicated aorist participle of παραπείθω ‘win over, persuade’, with the α of παρα- lost before the next syllable. πτολίπορθος is ‘city-sacking’ (πτόλις ‘city’ + πέρθω ‘sack’), the epithet of Odysseus, translated each time. Agamemnon’s speech ends with the second line of this unit, line 119.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε ψυχὴ προσεφώνεεν Ἀμφιμέδοντος·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute psychē prosephōneen Amphimedontos·
sentences.l: Him in turn the soul of Amphimedon spoke to:
sentences.i: The soul of Amphimedon spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula of reply. τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, Agamemnon, and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the change of speaker. ψυχή is ‘soul’, the subject, so the genitive Ἀμφιμέδοντος names whose soul it is. προσεφώνεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω with the movable -ν; it is rendered ‘spoke to’, not ‘addressed’ (the English of προσέειπε and προσέφη). The speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε, ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον,
μέμνημαι τάδε πάντα, διοτρεφές, ὡς ἀγορεύεις·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē kydiste, anax andrōn Agamemnon,
memnēmai tade panta, diotrephes, hōs agoreueis·
sentences.l:
“Atreus’ son, most glorious, lord of men, Agamemnon,
I remember all this, Zeus-nurtured one, as you speak:
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, I remember all this, Zeus-nurtured one, just as you say:
sentences.n: Amphimedon answers. The first line is a string of vocatives: Ἀτρεΐδη ‘son of Atreus’, κύδιστε ‘most glorious’ (the superlative of κυδρός), ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ and the name; διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured one’ follows in the second line. μέμνημαι is a perfect with present sense, ‘I remember’, with τάδε πάντα ‘all this’ as object, and ὡς ἀγορεύεις is ‘as you speak’. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ ἐγὼ εὖ μάλα πάντα καὶ ἀτρεκέως καταλέξω,
ἡμετέρου θανάτοιο κακὸν τέλος, οἷον ἐτύχθη.
sentences.tr:
soi d’ egō eu mala panta kai atrekeōs katalexō,
hēmeterou thanatoio kakon telos, hoion etychthē.
sentences.l:
And to you I, very well, all things, and exactly, will recount,
the evil end of our death, of what sort it came about.
sentences.i: And I shall recount it all to you, well and exactly: the evil end of our death, and what sort of end it was.
sentences.n: σοί is the dative ‘to you’, placed first and answered by ἐγώ ‘I’. καταλέξω is the future of καταλέγω ‘recount in order’, ἀτρεκέως is ‘exactly’, and εὖ μάλα ‘very well, thoroughly’. κακὸν τέλος, ‘the evil end’, stands in apposition to πάντα. οἷον ἐτύχθη is an exclamatory relative, ‘of what sort it was’: ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω ‘make, bring about’. ἡμετέρου is ‘our’.

sentences.t: μνώμεθ’ Ὀδυσσῆος δὴν οἰχομένοιο δάμαρτα·
sentences.tr: mnōmeth’ Odyssēos dēn oichomenoio damarta·
sentences.l: We were wooing the wife of Odysseus, long gone;
sentences.i: We were courting the wife of Odysseus, who had been gone so long;
sentences.n: μνώμεθ’ is μνώμεθα, the imperfect middle of μνάομαι ‘woo’ without the augment: ‘we were wooing’. δάμαρτα is the accusative of δάμαρ ‘wife’. δὴν οἰχομένοιο is a genitive participle of οἴχομαι agreeing with Ὀδυσσῆος, ‘long gone’. Ὀδυσσῆος is spelled with σσ here and as Ὀδυσῆος later in this part; the metre can need either form.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ οὔτ’ ἠρνεῖτο στυγερὸν γάμον οὔτ’ ἐτελεύτα,
ἡμῖν φραζομένη θάνατον καὶ κῆρα μέλαιναν,
ἀλλὰ δόλον τόνδ’ ἄλλον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μερμήριξε·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ out’ ērneito stygeron gamon out’ eteleuta,
hēmin phrazomenē thanaton kai kēra melainan,
alla dolon tond’ allon eni phresi mermērixe·
sentences.l:
And she neither refused the hateful marriage nor brought it to an end,
planning for us death and black death-fate,
but this other trick in her mind she devised:
sentences.i: She neither refused the marriage she hated nor brought it to an end, planning for us death and the black spirit of death, but she thought up this further trick in her mind:
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is the pronoun, ‘and she’. ἠρνεῖτο and ἐτελεύτα are imperfects of ἀρνέομαι ‘refuse’ and τελευτάω ‘bring to completion’, in the pair οὔτ’ … οὔτ’ ‘neither … nor’; στυγερόν is ‘hateful’. φραζομένη is the middle participle of φράζω ‘plan, contrive’, with κῆρα μέλαιναν ‘the black death-spirit’ (κήρ, the power of death, not κῆρ ‘heart’). ἀλλά … μερμήριξε is ‘but she thought up’, the unaugmented aorist of μερμηρίζω, and τόνδ’ ἄλλον ‘this other’ means a further trick. The ano teleia introduces the trick.

sentences.t:
στησαμένη μέγαν ἱστὸν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ὕφαινε,
λεπτὸν καὶ περίμετρον·
sentences.tr:
stēsamenē megan histon eni megaroisin hyphaine,
lepton kai perimetron·
sentences.l:
setting up a great loom in the halls, she was weaving,
fine and very large;
sentences.i: she set up a great loom in her halls and went on weaving a web, fine and very large;
sentences.n: στησαμένη is the aorist middle participle of ἵστημι, ‘setting up for herself’. ἱστός is the upright loom and, by extension, the web on it, and the adjectives λεπτόν ‘fine’ and περίμετρον ‘of very great size’ suit the web. ὕφαινε is the imperfect of ὑφαίνω ‘weave’, so the work went on, and μεγάροισιν is a plural for the rooms of one house. The ano teleia after περίμετρον ends the unit in the middle of line 130.

sentences.t: ἄφαρ δ’ ἡμῖν μετέειπε·
sentences.tr: aphar d’ hēmin meteeipe·
sentences.l: and straightway she spoke among us:
sentences.i: and at once she spoke among us:
sentences.n: ἄφαρ is ‘at once’. μετέειπε is ‘spoke among’, a verb that introduces a speech to a company, and ἡμῖν is ‘to us’, the suitors. Penelope’s own words, quoted inside Amphimedon’s, begin in the next unit and are set in single quotation marks.

sentences.t:
κοῦροι ἐμοὶ μνηστῆρες, ἐπεὶ θάνε δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
μίμνετ’ ἐπειγόμενοι τὸν ἐμὸν γάμον, εἰς ὅ κε φᾶρος
ἐκτελέσω, μή μοι μεταμώνια νήματ’ ὄληται,
sentences.tr:
kouroi emoi mnēstēres, epei thane dios Odysseus,
mimnet’ epeigomenoi ton emon gamon, eis ho ke pharos
ektelesō, mē moi metamōnia nēmat’ olētai,
sentences.l:
‘Young men, my suitors, since heavenly Odysseus has died,
wait, eager though you are for my marriage, until this robe
I finish, lest my threads should perish, gone to waste,
sentences.i: ‘Young men, my suitors, since heavenly Odysseus is dead, wait, eager though you are for my marriage, until I have finished this robe, so that my spinning may not be wasted and lost,
sentences.n: Single quotation marks set off Penelope’s words inside Amphimedon’s speech. κοῦροι is ‘young men’. θάνε is the unaugmented aorist of θνῄσκω, ‘has died’. μίμνετ’ is μίμνετε, ‘wait’, and ἐπειγόμενοι ‘pressing for, eager for’ takes γάμον as its object. εἰς ὅ κε with the subjunctive ἐκτελέσω is ‘until I finish’. φᾶρος is a large cloth, and μεταμώνια, ‘wasted’, is usually connected with ἄνεμος ‘wind’: ‘gone with the wind’. νήματ’ is νήματα ‘threads’. The sentence runs for seven lines, so it is cut at this comma.

sentences.t:
Λαέρτῃ ἥρωϊ ταφήϊον, εἰς ὅτε κέν μιν
μοῖρ’ ὀλοὴ καθέλῃσι τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο,
μή τίς μοι κατὰ δῆμον Ἀχαιϊάδων νεμεσήσῃ,
αἴ κεν ἄτερ σπείρου κεῖται πολλὰ κτεατίσσας.
sentences.tr:
Laertēi hērōï taphēïon, eis hote ken min
moir’ oloē kathelēisi tanēlegeos thanatoio,
mē tis moi kata dēmon Achaiïadōn nemesēsēi,
ai ken ater speirou keitai polla kteatissas.
sentences.l:
for the hero Laertes a burial-cloth, against the time when him
the deadly fate takes down of death that lays-at-length,
lest anyone in the land of the Achaean women feel indignation at me,
if without a winding-sheet he should lie, having won much.’
sentences.i: a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day when the deadly fate of death that lays men at length shall take him down, so that none of the Achaean women in the land may feel indignation at me, if he should lie without a winding-sheet, a man who had won great possessions.’
sentences.n: ταφήϊον, ‘for burial’, stands in apposition to φᾶρος: the cloth is to be Laertes’ shroud. εἰς ὅτε κέν with the subjunctive is ‘against the time when’, μιν is Laertes, and καθέλῃσι is the aorist subjunctive of καθαιρέω ‘take down’. μοῖρ’ ὀλοή is ‘the deadly fate’. The meaning of τανηλεγής is not known: ‘laying men at full length’ (τανυ- ‘stretched’ + λέγω ‘lay’) and ‘bringing long sorrow’ (from ἄλγος) are both ancient guesses, and the English follows the first. αἴ κεν is ‘if’; ἄτερ takes the genitive σπείρου ‘winding-sheet’, and πολλὰ κτεατίσσας is ‘having acquired much’. Penelope’s words end here, so the single quotation mark closes.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἡμῖν δ’ αὖτ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hēmin d’ aut’ epepeitheto thymos agēnōr.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and then our own lordly heart was persuaded;
sentences.i: So she said, and our own proud hearts were won over.
sentences.n: ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, the imperfect middle of φημί, ‘she spoke’, and it closes Penelope’s speech; Amphimedon’s own account now resumes. ἡμῖν is a dative of interest, ‘to us’, so ‘our’ with θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ, the fixed pair, ‘lordly heart’ in the literal layer and ‘proud hearts’ in the idiomatic one, here said of the suitors’ own hearts. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘then, in turn’. ἐπεπείθετο is the imperfect of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey, be persuaded’, with the augment placed after the preverb ἐπι-: it has the stem πείθ- and is not a perfect.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα καὶ ἠματίη μὲν ὑφαίνεσκεν μέγαν ἱστόν,
νύκτας δ’ ἀλλύεσκεν, ἐπεὶ δαΐδας παραθεῖτο.
sentences.tr:
entha kai ēmatiē men hyphainesken megan histon,
nyktas d’ allyesken, epei daïdas paratheito.
sentences.l:
There by day she would weave the great web,
but by nights she would unravel it, when she had set torches beside her.
sentences.i: There by day she would weave her great web, and by night unravel it again, once she had placed torches beside her.
sentences.n: ἠματίη is ‘by day’, and νύκτας, an accusative of time, ‘by night’; the two halves of the trick are set side by side. ὑφαίνεσκεν and ἀλλύεσκεν are iterative imperfects in -σκ-, ‘she would weave’, ‘she would unravel’, marking repeated action. ἀλλύω is ‘undo’, the same word as ἀναλύω. δαΐδας παραθεῖτο is an aorist optative in a clause of repeated circumstance, ‘whenever she had set torches beside her’.

sentences.t: ὣς τρίετες μὲν ἔληθε δόλῳ καὶ ἔπειθεν Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr: hōs trietes men elēthe dolōi kai epeithen Achaious·
sentences.l: So for three years, by her trick, she escaped notice and deceived the Achaeans;
sentences.i: So for three years her trick went undetected, and she deceived the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ sums up the routine. τρίετες is an adverbial accusative of duration, ‘for three years’. ἔληθε is the imperfect of λήθω, a poetic by-form of λανθάνω, ‘escaped notice’, with the dative δόλῳ ‘by a trick’; ἔπειθεν is the imperfect of πείθω, here ‘deceived’. Ἀχαιούς, ‘the Achaeans’, is what the suitors call themselves and their fellows.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε τέτρατον ἦλθεν ἔτος καὶ ἐπήλυθον ὧραι,
μηνῶν φθινόντων, περὶ δ’ ἤματα πόλλ’ ἐτελέσθη,
καὶ τότε δή τις ἔειπε γυναικῶν, ἣ σάφα ᾔδη,
καὶ τήν γ’ ἀλλύουσαν ἐφεύρομεν ἀγλαὸν ἱστόν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote tetraton ēlthen etos kai epēlython hōrai,
mēnōn phthinontōn, peri d’ ēmata poll’ etelesthē,
kai tote dē tis eeipe gynaikōn, hē sapha ēidē,
kai tēn g’ allyousan epheuromen aglaon histon.
sentences.l:
But when the fourth year came, and the seasons passed by,
as the months were waning, and many days were brought round to their end,
then indeed one of the women spoke, one who knew it clearly,
and we caught her, in the act, undoing the splendid web.
sentences.i: But when the fourth year came round and the seasons had passed, as the months waned and many days had run their course, one of the women, who knew the truth of it, spoke out, and we caught her undoing the splendid web.
sentences.n: ἦλθεν ἔτος is ‘the year came’, ἐπήλυθον an aorist of ἐπέρχομαι (Attic ἐπῆλθον), and ὧραι ‘the seasons’. μηνῶν φθινόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘the months waning’. περὶ … ἐτελέσθη is a tmesis for περιετελέσθη, ‘were brought round to their end’: the days came full circle. ἔειπε is ‘spoke’, and ἣ σάφα ᾔδη is ‘who knew it clearly’, ᾔδη being the pluperfect of οἶδα. ἐφεύρομεν is ‘we found, caught’, and ἀλλύουσαν ‘undoing’. The sentence runs to the full stop at the end of line 145.

sentences.t: ὣς τὸ μὲν ἐξετέλεσσε καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλουσ’, ὑπ’ ἀνάγκης.
sentences.tr: hōs to men exetelesse kai ouk ethelous’, hyp’ anankēs.
sentences.l: So that she finished, even unwilling, under compulsion;
sentences.i: So she finished the web, against her will, under compulsion.
sentences.n: τό is the pronoun ‘it’, the web, not the article. ἐξετέλεσσε is the aorist of ἐκτελέω ‘bring to completion’. οὐκ ἐθέλουσ’ is the participle ‘not willing’, with concessive force, ‘even though unwilling’, and ὑπ’ ἀνάγκης is ‘under compulsion’.

sentences.t:
εὖθ’ ἡ φᾶρος ἔδειξεν, ὑφήνασα μέγαν ἱστόν,
πλύνασ’, ἠελίῳ ἐναλίγκιον ἠὲ σελήνῃ,
καὶ τότε δή ῥ’ Ὀδυσῆα κακός ποθεν ἤγαγε δαίμων
ἀγροῦ ἐπ’ ἐσχατιήν, ὅθι δώματα ναῖε συβώτης.
sentences.tr:
euth’ hē pharos edeixen, hyphēnasa megan histon,
plynas’, ēeliōi enalinkion ēe selēnēi,
kai tote dē rh’ Odysēa kakos pothen ēgage daimōn
agrou ep’ eschatiēn, hothi dōmata naie sybōtēs.
sentences.l:
When she showed the robe, having woven the great web,
having washed it, like to the sun or to the moon,
then indeed some evil power from somewhere led Odysseus
to the edge of the farmland, where the swineherd dwelt in his house.
sentences.i: When she showed the robe, once she had woven the great web and washed it, shining like the sun or the moon, then some evil power brought Odysseus from somewhere to the edge of the farmland, where the swineherd lived.
sentences.n: εὖθ’ is ‘when’, and ἡ is the pronoun ‘she’, Penelope. ὑφήνασα and πλύνασ’ are aorist participles of ὑφαίνω ‘weave’ and πλύνω ‘wash’. ἐναλίγκιον ‘like to’ is neuter to agree with φᾶρος and takes the datives ἠελίῳ … σελήνῃ. καὶ τότε δή ‘and then indeed’ is the turn of the story. ποθεν is the indefinite ‘from somewhere’; δαίμων is ‘some power’, an unnamed divine power, here κακός ‘evil’ from the suitors’ side. ἀγροῦ ἐπ’ ἐσχατιήν is ‘to the edge of the farmland’, and ναῖε is the unaugmented imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦλθεν φίλος υἱὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο,
ἐκ Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος ἰὼν σὺν νηῒ μελαίνῃ·
sentences.tr:
enth’ ēlthen philos huios Odyssēos theioio,
ek Pylou ēmathoentos iōn syn nēï melainēi·
sentences.l:
There came the dear son of divine Odysseus,
from sandy Pylos going with a black ship;
sentences.i: There came the dear son of divine Odysseus, from sandy Pylos in his black ship;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘there’. φίλος υἱός is ‘dear son’, and Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο is ‘of divine Odysseus’: θεῖος is ‘divine’, not the δῖος ‘heavenly’ of other lines. The unnamed son is Telemachus. ἐκ Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος is ‘from sandy Pylos’, ἠμαθόεις being the stock epithet. ἰών is the participle of εἶμι ‘go, come’, and σὺν νηῒ μελαίνῃ is ‘with a black ship’, νηῒ being the dative of ναῦς. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ μνηστῆρσιν θάνατον κακὸν ἀρτύναντε
ἵκοντο προτὶ ἄστυ περικλυτόν, ἦ τοι Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὕστερος, αὐτὰρ Τηλέμαχος πρόσθ’ ἡγεμόνευε.
sentences.tr:
tō de mnēstērsin thanaton kakon artynante
hikonto proti asty periklyton, ē toi Odysseus
hysteros, autar Tēlemachos prosth’ hēgemoneue.
sentences.l:
And the two, for the suitors an evil death having prepared,
came to the very-famous town, Odysseus indeed
later, but Telemachus in front led the way.
sentences.i: The two of them, having prepared an evil death for the suitors, came to the very famous town, Odysseus coming later, but Telemachus leading the way in front.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual ‘the two’, Odysseus and Telemachus, and ἀρτύναντε is the dual aorist participle of ἀρτύνω ‘prepare, arrange’. The dual subject takes the plural verb ἵκοντο, the unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘arrive’. προτί is πρός ‘to’, ἄστυ ‘town’, and περικλυτόν ‘very famous’ (περι- intensive + κλυτός). ἦ τοι … αὐτάρ is ‘on the one hand … but’. ὕστερος is ‘later, last’, πρόσθ’ is πρόσθε ‘in front’, and ἡγεμόνευε ‘led the way’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ συβώτης ἦγε κακὰ χροῒ εἵματ’ ἔχοντα,
πτωχῷ λευγαλέῳ ἐναλίγκιον ἠδὲ γέροντι
σκηπτόμενον· τὰ δὲ λυγρὰ περὶ χροῒ εἵματα ἕστο·
sentences.tr:
ton de sybōtēs ēge kaka chroï heimat’ echonta,
ptōchōi leugaleōi enalinkion ēde geronti
skēptomenon· ta de lygra peri chroï heimata hesto·
sentences.i: And the swineherd was leading him, wearing shabby clothes on his body, looking like a pitiful beggar and an old man, leaning on a staff; he wore the grievous clothes on his body;
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, Odysseus, object of ἦγε ‘was leading’; ἔχοντα and σκηπτόμενον agree with it. κακά ‘bad’ and λυγρά ‘grievous’ describe the same clothes, and χροΐ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’. ἐναλίγκιον ‘like to’ takes the dative πτωχῷ λευγαλέῳ ἠδὲ γέροντι, ‘a pitiful beggar and an old man’. σκηπτόμενον is ‘leaning on’ (a staff, understood). ἕστο is the pluperfect middle of ἕννυμι, ‘he was wearing’. The ano teleia at the end of line 158 ends the unit.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἡμείων δύνατο γνῶναι τὸν ἐόντα
ἐξαπίνης προφανέντ’, οὐδ’ οἳ προγενέστεροι ἦσαν,
ἀλλ’ ἔπεσίν τε κακοῖσιν ἐνίσσομεν ἠδὲ βολῇσιν.
sentences.tr:
oude tis hēmeiōn dynato gnōnai ton eonta
exapinēs prophanent’, oud’ hoi progenesteroi ēsan,
all’ epesin te kakoisin enissomen ēde bolēisin.
sentences.l:
And none of us was able to recognize him, being who he was,
suddenly appearing, not even those who were older,
but with evil words we rebuked him, and with throws.
sentences.i: None of us could recognize him for who he was when he appeared so suddenly, not even those who were older, but we abused him with insulting words and with missiles.
sentences.n: ἡμείων is ἡμέων, the uncontracted genitive ‘of us’. δύνατο is the imperfect of δύναμαι without the augment (Attic ἠδύνατο), and γνῶναι is ‘to recognize’; τὸν ἐόντα is ‘him, being (who he was)’. ἐξαπίνης is ‘suddenly’, and προφανέντ’ the passive aorist participle of προφαίνω ‘show forth’. οὐδ’ οἳ προγενέστεροι ἦσαν is ‘not even those who were older’. ἐνίσσομεν is a by-form of the verb ‘rebuke, abuse’ (ἐνίπτω), with the datives ἔπεσιν κακοῖσιν ‘with evil words’ and βολῇσιν ‘with throws’, the missiles flung at him.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ τῆος ἐτόλμα ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἑοῖσι
βαλλόμενος καὶ ἐνισσόμενος τετληότι θυμῷ·
sentences.tr:
autar ho tēos etolma eni megaroisin heoisi
ballomenos kai enissomenos tetlēoti thymōi·
sentences.l:
But he meanwhile held out in his own halls,
being struck and being rebuked, with enduring heart;
sentences.i: But he held out meanwhile in his own halls, pelted and abused, with an enduring heart;
sentences.n: τῆος is ‘meanwhile’, an epic form of τέως, and ἐτόλμα the imperfect of τολμάω, ‘held out, endured’. ἑοῖσι is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, ‘his own’, agreeing with μεγάροισιν: easily mistaken for a pronoun. βαλλόμενος and ἐνισσόμενος are passive participles, ‘being struck’ and ‘being rebuked’. τετληότι θυμῷ, ‘with enduring heart’, is the phrase for one who holds out; τετληότι is the perfect participle of τλάω ‘endure’. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή μιν ἔγειρε Διὸς νοός αἰγιόχοιο,
σὺν μὲν Τηλεμάχῳ περικαλλέα τεύχε’ ἀείρας
ἐς θάλαμον κατέθηκε καὶ ἐκλήϊσεν ὀχῆας,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē min egeire Dios noos aigiochoio,
syn men Tēlemachōi perikallea teuche’ aeiras
es thalamon katethēke kai eklēïsen ochēas,
sentences.l:
But when indeed him roused the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus,
with Telemachus the very fair armour having lifted up
into a chamber he put it away, and he shut the bolts,
sentences.i: But when the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus roused him, he took up the very fair armour together with Telemachus, put it away in a chamber, and shut the bolts,
sentences.n: ἔγειρε is the imperfect of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’. Its subject νοός, printed with the acute on the last syllable, is the nominative νόος ‘mind’: ‘the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus roused him’. μιν is ‘him’, Odysseus. αἰγιόχοιο is the genitive of αἰγίοχος ‘aegis-bearing’, an epithet of Zeus whose meaning is disputed. σὺν μὲν Τηλεμάχῳ goes with ἀείρας ‘having lifted up’, whose subject is Odysseus. περικαλλέα is ‘very fair’, and τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’. θάλαμον is ‘a chamber’, the inner storeroom; ἐκλήϊσεν is ‘shut’, and ὀχῆας ‘the bolts’. The comma carries the sentence into the next unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ ἣν ἄλοχον πολυκερδείῃσιν ἄνωγε
τόξον μνηστήρεσσι θέμεν πολιόν τε σίδηρον,
ἡμῖν αἰνομόροισιν ἀέθλια καὶ φόνου ἀρχήν.
sentences.tr:
autar ho hēn alochon polykerdeiēisin anōge
toxon mnēstēressi themen polion te sidēron,
hēmin ainomoroisin aethlia kai phonou archēn.
sentences.l:
but he, by many-gainful ways, his own wife bade
the bow for the suitors to set, and the grey iron,
for us, dread-fated, a contest and the beginning of slaughter.
sentences.i: while he, with his alertness to every advantage, bade his own wife set the bow and the grey iron before the suitors, as a contest and the beginning of slaughter for us, so grimly fated.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὁ is ‘but he’, Odysseus. ἣν ἄλοχον has ἣν as the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative: ‘his own wife’. πολυκερδείῃσιν is a rare plural noun in the dative, built like πολυκερδής on πολύ and κέρδος ‘gain, advantage’; ‘by many-gainful ways’ is the literal sense, and ‘with his alertness to every advantage’ the idiomatic one. ἄνωγε is ‘bade’: the third singular of the old perfect ἄνωγα ‘I bid’, which Homer also uses with past force (the pluperfect is ἠνώγει). θέμεν is the infinitive ‘to set’ (= θεῖναι). τόξον … πολιόν τε σίδηρον, ‘the bow and the grey iron’, are its objects. ἡμῖν αἰνομόροισιν is ‘for us, grimly fated’, and ἀέθλια ‘a contest’ and φόνου ἀρχήν ‘the beginning of slaughter’ are in apposition to the objects.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἡμείων δύνατο κρατεροῖο βιοῖο
νευρὴν ἐντανύσαι, πολλὸν δ’ ἐπιδευέες ἦμεν.
sentences.tr:
oude tis hēmeiōn dynato krateroio bioio
neurēn entanysai, pollon d’ epideuees ēmen.
sentences.l:
And none of us was able of the strong bow
the string to string, and by much we were lacking.
sentences.i: And not one of us was able to string the strong bow, for we fell far short.
sentences.n: βιοῖο is the genitive of βιός ‘bow’, a poetic word that differs from βίος ‘life’ only in the accent; it depends on νευρήν ‘bowstring’, the object of ἐντανύσαι, ‘to string’ (from τανύω ‘stretch’). κρατεροῖο is ‘strong’. πολλὸν is the adverb ‘by much’, and ἐπιδευέες ἦμεν is ‘we were lacking’, with ‘in strength’ understood.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε χεῖρας ἵκανεν Ὀδυσσῆος μέγα τόξον,
ἔνθ’ ἡμεῖς μὲν πάντες ὁμοκλέομεν ἐπέεσσι
τόξον μὴ δόμεναι, μηδ’ εἰ μάλα πολλ’ ἀγορεύοι·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote cheiras hikanen Odyssēos mega toxon,
enth’ hēmeis men pantes homokleomen epeessi
toxon mē domenai, mēd’ ei mala poll’ agoreuoi·
sentences.i: But when the great bow reached the hands of Odysseus, then we all shouted out that the bow must not be given, no matter how much he said;
sentences.n: ἵκανεν is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’, with χεῖρας as its goal, so ‘the great bow came to the hands of Odysseus’. ὁμοκλέομεν is ‘we shouted’, with ἐπέεσσι ‘with words’. τόξον μὴ δόμεναι is the infinitive of an indirect command after ὁμοκλέομεν, ‘(that) the bow not be given’ (δόμεναι = δοῦναι, ‘to give’); neither the giver nor the receiver is named, so the English turns it passive. μηδ’ εἰ … ἀγορεύοι is ‘not even if he should speak much’, an optative after εἰ. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχος δέ μιν οἶος ἐποτρύνων ἐκέλευσεν.
sentences.tr: Tēlemachos de min oios epotrynōn ekeleusen.
sentences.l: But Telemachus, him, alone, urging on, ordered.
sentences.i: But Telemachus alone urged him on and gave the order.
sentences.n: μιν is ‘him’, Odysseus, and οἶος ‘alone’ agrees with Τηλέμαχος: Telemachus alone took the other side. ἐποτρύνων is ‘urging on’, and ἐκέλευσεν ‘ordered’; the Greek gives no object for the order and does not say what it was.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ δέξατο χειρὶ πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ῥηϊδίως δ’ ἐτάνυσσε βιόν, διὰ δ’ ἧκε σιδήρου,
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰών, ταχέας δ’ ἐκχεύατ’ ὀϊστοὺς
δεινὸν παπταίνων, βάλε δ’ Ἀντίνοον βασιλῆα.
sentences.tr:
autar ho dexato cheiri polytlas dios Odysseus,
rhēïdiōs d’ etanysse bion, dia d’ hēke sidērou,
stē d’ ar’ ep’ oudon iōn, tacheas d’ ekcheuat’ oïstous
deinon paptainōn, bale d’ Antinoon basilēa.
sentences.l:
But he took it in his hand, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
and easily strung the bow, and sent an arrow through the iron,
and he stood on the threshold, going, and poured out the swift arrows,
peering about dreadfully, and struck Antinous the king.
sentences.i: But much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus took it in his hand and easily strung the bow and shot through the iron; he went and stood on the threshold and poured out the swift arrows, peering about with a dread look, and struck Antinous the king.
sentences.n: δέξατο is the aorist of δέχομαι ‘take’, with χειρί ‘in his hand’. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is the name-formula ‘much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus’. ῥηϊδίως is ‘easily’; ἐτάνυσσε is the aorist of τανύω ‘string’ (with σσ), and βιόν the accusative of βιός ‘bow’. διὰ δ’ ἧκε σιδήρου is a tmesis: ‘sent through the iron’, with an arrow understood as object. στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰών is ‘and he went and stood on the threshold’. ἐκχεύατ’ is the aorist middle of ἐκχέω ‘pour out’, and ταχέας ‘swift’. δεινὸν παπταίνων is ‘peering about dreadfully’, the neuter adjective used as an adverb. βάλε is the aorist of βάλλω ‘strike’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ ἄλλοις ἐφίει βέλεα στονόεντα,
ἄντα τιτυσκόμενος·
sentences.tr:
autar epeit’ allois ephiei belea stonoenta,
anta tityskomenos·
sentences.l:
And then at others he kept sending arrows full of groaning,
aiming straight at them;
sentences.i: And then he kept sending arrows that brought groaning at the others, aiming straight at them;
sentences.n: ἐφίει is the imperfect of ἐφίημι ‘send at’, so ‘he kept sending’, with the dative ἄλλοις ‘at others’. βέλεα is ‘missiles, arrows’, and στονόεντα ‘full of groaning’ (στόνος ‘groan’ + -όεις). ἄντα τιτυσκόμενος is ‘aiming straight at (them)’. The ano teleia, in the middle of line 181, ends the unit.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἀγχιστῖνοι ἔπιπτον.
sentences.tr: toi d’ anchistinoi epipton.
sentences.l: and they, in close succession, fell.
sentences.i: and they fell one close upon another.
sentences.n: τοί is the old form of the plural ‘they’. ἔπιπτον is the imperfect of πίπτω ‘fall’. ἀγχιστῖνοι is a rare word built on ἄγχι ‘near’: ‘close together, in close succession’ is the sense the context gives, but the exact meaning is not known.

sentences.t: γνωτὸν δ’ ἦν ὅ ῥά τίς σφι θεῶν ἐπιτάρροθος ἦεν·
sentences.tr: gnōton d’ ēn ho rha tis sphi theōn epitarrothos ēen·
sentences.l: And known it was that some one of the gods was a helper to them;
sentences.i: It was plain that one of the gods was helping them;
sentences.n: γνωτόν is ‘known, plain’, and ἦν ‘it was’: the clause is ‘it was plain that …’. ὅ is the conjunction ‘that’, with ῥα the particle of lively narration. τίς θεῶν is ‘some one of the gods’, and σφι ‘to them’, the killers. ἐπιτάρροθος is ‘helper’, a rare word whose formation is obscure; ἦεν is the epic imperfect ‘was’. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα γὰρ κατὰ δώματ’ ἐπισπόμενοι μένεϊ σφῷ
κτεῖνον ἐπιστροφάδην, τῶν δὲ στόνος ὤρνυτ’ ἀεικὴς
κράτων τυπτομένων, δάπεδον δ’ ἅπαν αἵματι θῦεν.
sentences.tr:
autika gar kata dōmat’ epispomenoi meneï sphōi
kteinon epistrophadēn, tōn de stonos ōrnyt’ aeikēs
kratōn typtomenōn, dapedon d’ hapan haimati thyen.
sentences.l:
For at once through the house, following their own strength,
they were killing, turning from one to another, and of them a groaning rose, unseemly,
of heads being struck, and the whole floor seethed with blood.
sentences.i: For at once they went through the house, following their own strength, and killed, wheeling from one man to the next, and an unseemly groaning rose from their stricken heads, and the whole floor seethed with blood.
sentences.n: αὐτίκα γάρ, ‘for at once’, gives the proof of the god’s help. ἐπισπόμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἐφέπομαι ‘follow up, press on’; μένεϊ σφῷ is a dative, the object of the participle (ἕπομαι takes the dative), so ‘following their own strength’, σφῷ being the possessive ‘their own’; ‘with their own strength’ is the other possible reading. κτεῖνον is the imperfect ‘were killing’, and ἐπιστροφάδην an adverb, ‘turning from one man to the next’. τῶν is ‘of them’, στόνος ‘groaning’, ἀεικής ‘unseemly’; κράτων τυπτομένων is a genitive absolute, ‘heads being struck’, κράτων being the genitive plural of κάρ ‘head’. θῦεν is the imperfect of θύω ‘rush, seethe’, without the augment.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἡμεῖς, Ἀγάμεμνον, ἀπωλόμεθ’, ὧν ἔτι καὶ νῦν
σώματ’ ἀκηδέα κεῖται ἐνὶ μεγάροις Ὀδυσῆος·
sentences.tr:
hōs hēmeis, Agamemnon, apōlometh’, hōn eti kai nyn
sōmat’ akēdea keitai eni megarois Odysēos·
sentences.l:
So we, Agamemnon, perished, of whom still even now
the bodies lie uncared for in the halls of Odysseus;
sentences.i: So we perished, Agamemnon, and our bodies still lie uncared for even now in the halls of Odysseus;
sentences.n: ὣς ἡμεῖς … ἀπωλόμεθ’ is ‘so we perished’, ἀπωλόμεθ’ being the aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι, elided. ὧν is the relative ‘of whom’, the genitive of possession with σώματ’, ‘whose bodies’. ἔτι καὶ νῦν is ‘still even now’. ἀκηδέα, neuter plural of ἀκηδής, is ‘uncared for’ (ἀ- + κῆδος ‘care’), and κεῖται, a singular verb with a neuter plural subject, is ‘lie’. The halls are Ὀδυσῆος ‘of Odysseus’, spelled with one σ.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω ἴσασι φίλοι κατὰ δώμαθ’ ἑκάστου,
οἵ κ’ ἀπονίψαντες μέλανα βρότον ἐξ ὠτειλέων
κατθέμενοι γοάοιεν· ὃ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ θανόντων.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō isasi philoi kata dōmath’ hekastou,
hoi k’ aponipsantes melana broton ex ōteileōn
katthemenoi goaoien· ho gar geras esti thanontōn.
sentences.l:
For not yet do they know, the dear ones, in the house of each,
who having washed off the dark gore from the wounds
and laid them out would lament; for that is the prize of the dead.”
sentences.i: For their dear ones in each man’s house do not yet know it — those who would wash the dark gore from the wounds, lay the bodies out and mourn; for that is the prize of honour that belongs to the dead.”
sentences.n: οὐ … πω ἴσασι is ‘they do not yet know’ (third plural of οἶδα). φίλοι are ‘the dear ones’, the kin; κατὰ δώμαθ’ ἑκάστου is ‘in the house of each’. οἵ κ’ … γοάοιεν is a relative clause with κε and the optative, ‘who would lament’ (if they knew); ἀπονίψαντες ‘having washed off’ and κατθέμενοι ‘having laid out’ are aorist participles. μέλανα βρότον is ‘dark gore’, βρότος being blood from a wound, not βροτός ‘mortal’; ὠτειλέων is the genitive plural of ὠτειλή ‘wound’. ὃ γὰρ γέρας ἐστί is ‘for that is the prize of honour’, the honour due to θανόντων ‘the dead’. Amphimedon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε ψυχὴ προσεφώνεεν Ἀτρεΐδαο·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute psychē prosephōneen Atreïdao·
sentences.l: Him in turn the soul of Atreus’ son spoke to:
sentences.i: The soul of the son of Atreus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The reply-formula again. τόν is Amphimedon, αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the change of speaker, and προσεφώνεεν is ‘spoke to’, with the movable -ν. Ἀτρεΐδαο is a genitive in -αο, ‘of the son of Atreus’, Agamemnon, written here with a diaeresis on the ι. The speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὄλβιε Λαέρταο πάϊ, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
ἦ ἄρα σὺν μεγάλῃ ἀρετῇ ἐκτήσω ἄκοιτιν.
sentences.tr:
olbie Laertao paï, polymēchan’ Odysseu,
ē ara syn megalēi aretēi ektēsō akoitin.
sentences.l:
“Prosperous son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
truly then with great excellence you acquired a wife.
sentences.i: “Prosperous son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, you have indeed won a wife of great excellence.
sentences.n: Agamemnon answers. ὄλβιε and πολυμήχαν’ are vocatives, and Λαέρταο πάϊ is ‘son of Laertes’, with the genitive in -αο and πάϊ the vocative of παῖς. ὄλβιος is ‘prosperous’, and πολυμήχανος ‘many-devising’ in the literal layer and ‘man of many devices’ in the idiomatic one. ἦ ἄρα is ‘truly then’. ἐκτήσω is the aorist middle of κτάομαι ‘acquire’, second singular. σὺν μεγάλῃ ἀρετῇ is ‘with great excellence’, the excellence being Penelope’s, as the next lines show.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἀγαθαὶ φρένες ἦσαν ἀμύμονι Πηνελοπείῃ,
κούρῃ Ἰκαρίου·
sentences.tr:
hōs agathai phrenes ēsan amymoni Pēnelopeiēi,
kourēi Ikariou·
sentences.l:
How good the wits were in blameless Penelope,
the daughter of Icarius;
sentences.i: How good was the sense of blameless Penelope, the daughter of Icarius;
sentences.n: ὡς is the exclamatory ‘how’. ἀγαθαὶ φρένες is ‘good wits’, φρένες being the seat of understanding, and ἦσαν ‘were’, with the dative of possession ἀμύμονι Πηνελοπείῃ (‘blameless Penelope had’), which the English puts as ‘in blameless Penelope’. The epithet ἀμύμων is always translated ‘blameless’; its real sense is not known. κούρῃ Ἰκαρίου is ‘daughter of Icarius’. The ano teleia, in the middle of line 195, ends the unit.

sentences.t:
ὡς εὖ μέμνητ’ Ὀδυσῆος,
ἀνδρὸς κουριδίου·
sentences.tr:
hōs eu memnēt’ Odysēos,
andros kouridiou·
sentences.l:
how well she remembers Odysseus,
her wedded husband;
sentences.i: how well she remembers Odysseus, her wedded husband;
sentences.n: ὡς εὖ is ‘how well’. μέμνητ’ is μέμνηται, a perfect with present sense, ‘she remembers’, taking the genitive Ὀδυσῆος. ἀνδρὸς κουριδίου is ‘her wedded husband’, in apposition to Ὀδυσῆος. The ano teleia, in the middle of line 196, ends the unit.

sentences.t:
τῷ οἱ κλέος οὔ ποτ’ ὀλεῖται
ἧς ἀρετῆς, τεύξουσι δ’ ἐπιχθονίοισιν ἀοιδὴν
ἀθάνατοι χαρίεσσαν ἐχέφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ,
sentences.tr:
tōi hoi kleos ou pot’ oleitai
hēs aretēs, teuxousi d’ epichthonioisin aoidēn
athanatoi chariessan echephroni Pēnelopeiēi,
sentences.l:
therefore for her the fame will never perish
of her excellence, and they will make for men upon the earth a song
the immortals, a graceful one, for sound-minded Penelope,
sentences.i: and so the fame of her excellence will never perish, and the immortals will make a graceful song for men who live on the earth in honour of sound-minded Penelope,
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘therefore’. οἱ is ‘for her’, the dative of interest, and κλέος ἧς ἀρετῆς is ‘the fame of her excellence’, ἧς being the possessive ‘her own’; ὀλεῖται is the future middle of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’. τεύξουσι is the future of τεύχω ‘make’, third plural, and its subject ἀθάνατοι ‘the immortals’ is set after the object. ἐπιχθονίοισιν is ‘for men upon the earth’, χαρίεσσαν ‘graceful’, and ἐχέφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ ‘for sound-minded Penelope’, a dative of advantage. The sentence from here to line 202 is more than six lines long, so it is cut at this comma.

sentences.t:
οὐχ ὡς Τυνδαρέου κούρη κακὰ μήσατο ἔργα,
κουρίδιον κτείνασα πόσιν, στυγερὴ δέ τ’ ἀοιδὴ
ἔσσετ’ ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους, χαλεπὴν δέ τε φῆμιν ὀπάσσει
θηλυτέρῃσι γυναιξί, καὶ ἥ κ’ εὐεργὸς ἔῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
ouch hōs Tyndareou kourē kaka mēsato erga,
kouridion kteinasa posin, stygerē de t’ aoidē
esset’ ep’ anthrōpous, chalepēn de te phēmin opassei
thēlyterēisi gynaixi, kai hē k’ euergos eēisin.
sentences.l:
not as the daughter of Tyndareus devised evil deeds,
her wedded husband having killed, and a hateful song
will be among men, and harsh talk it will bestow
on female women, even whichever may be well-working.”
sentences.i: not as the daughter of Tyndareus devised evil deeds, killing her wedded husband; a hateful song will be among men, and it will bestow harsh talk on women, even on one who does well.”
sentences.n: οὐχ ὡς is ‘not as’, the contrast. κούρη Τυνδαρέου is ‘the daughter of Tyndareus’, Agamemnon’s own wife Clytemnestra, whom the speech does not name. μήσατο is the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise’; κουρίδιον … πόσιν is ‘her wedded husband’. στυγερὴ ἀοιδή is ‘a hateful song’, ἔσσετ’ the epic future of εἰμί ‘will be’, and ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους ‘among men’. ὀπάσσει is the future of ὀπάζω ‘bestow’; its subject is the song or the woman, and the Greek does not mark the change; the English takes it to be the song. θηλυτέρῃσι γυναιξί, ‘female women’, is a fixed phrase for womankind; ἔῃσιν is the subjunctive of εἰμί, and εὐεργός ‘well-working’ means one who does well. Agamemnon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
ἑσταότ’ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοις, ὑπὸ κεύθεσι γαίης·
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon,
hestaot’ ein Aïdao domois, hypo keuthesi gaiēs·
sentences.l:
So they, such things to one another were saying,
standing in the houses of Hades, beneath the hiding-places of the earth;
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, standing in the halls of Hades, beneath the recesses of the earth;
sentences.n: ὣς οἱ μέν is ‘so they, on their side’: οἱ is the pronoun, not the article, and the two speakers are meant. The clause closes the scene in the underworld. τοιαῦτα … ἀγόρευον is ‘were saying such things’, an imperfect. ἑσταότ’ is the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, elided, most naturally from the dual ἑσταότε for the two speakers. εἰν is ἐν, and Ἀΐδαο δόμοις is ‘in the houses of Hades’. κεύθεσι is the dative plural of κεῦθος ‘hiding-place’, so ‘beneath the hiding-places of the earth’. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ ἐκ πόλιος κατέβαν, τάχα δ’ ἀγρὸν ἵκοντο
καλὸν Λαέρταο τετυγμένον, ὅν ῥά ποτ’ αὐτὸς
Λαέρτης κτεάτισσεν, ἐπεὶ μάλα πόλλ’ ἐμόγησεν.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei ek polios kateban, tacha d’ agron hikonto
kalon Laertao tetygmenon, hon rha pot’ autos
Laertēs kteatissen, epei mala poll’ emogēsen.
sentences.l:
And they, when out of the city they had gone down, soon reached the farm
fine of Laertes, wrought, which once he himself
Laertes won, since very much he had toiled.
sentences.i: And when they had come down out of the city, they soon reached the fine, well-wrought farm of Laertes, which Laertes himself had once won by his great labour.
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ is ‘and they’, Odysseus and those with him. κατέβαν is the athematic aorist, with the augment, for κατέβησαν ‘went down’, and ἐκ πόλιος ‘out of the city’. τάχα is ‘soon’, ἵκοντο ‘reached’. ἀγρὸν καλὸν Λαέρταο τετυγμένον is ‘the fine farm of Laertes, well-wrought’: τετυγμένον is the perfect passive participle of τεύχω ‘make’, here ‘well made, well kept’. ὅν ῥά ποτ’ αὐτὸς Λαέρτης κτεάτισσεν is ‘which Laertes himself once won’, κτεατίζω being ‘acquire’, and ἐμόγησεν is the aorist of μογέω ‘toil’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα οἱ οἶκος ἔην, περὶ δὲ κλίσιον θέε πάντη,
ἐν τῷ σιτέσκοντο καὶ ἵζανον ἠδὲ ἴαυον
δμῶες ἀναγκαῖοι, τοί οἱ φίλα ἐργάζοντο.
sentences.tr:
entha hoi oikos eēn, peri de klision thee pantē,
en tōi siteskonto kai hizanon ēde iauon
dmōes anankaioi, toi hoi phila ergazonto.
sentences.l:
There for him was a house, and around it a shed ran on every side,
in which they used to eat and sit and sleep,
servants of compulsion, who worked for him kindly.
sentences.i: There he had a house, and a shed ran all around it, in which they used to eat and sit and sleep, the bound servants, who worked for him with a good will.
sentences.n: ἔνθα οἱ οἶκος ἔην is ‘there was a house of his’, the dative οἱ being the dative of possession. κλίσιον is a rare word from the root of κλίνω ‘lean’; its exact structure is not known, and ‘shed’ is only a working guess. The Greek gives no more than that it ran round (θέε, ‘ran’) the house on every side (πάντη). σιτέσκοντο, ἵζανον and ἴαυον are imperfects, the first with the iterative -σκ-: ‘they used to eat, sit and sleep’. δμῶες ἀναγκαῖοι is ‘servants of compulsion’, that is bondsmen, and τοί is the relative ‘who’. φίλα ἐργάζοντο is ‘worked kindly’, φίλα being a neuter plural used as an adverb.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ γυνὴ Σικελὴ γρηῢς πέλεν, ἥ ῥα γέροντα
ἐνδυκέως κομέεσκεν ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ, νόσφι πόληος.
sentences.tr:
en de gynē Sikelē grēÿs pelen, hē rha geronta
endykeōs komeesken ep’ agrou, nosphi polēos.
sentences.l:
And in it a Sicel woman, an old woman, was, who the old man
kindly used to tend on the farm, apart from the city.
sentences.i: In the house lived a Sicel woman, an old one, who kindly used to look after the old man there on the farm, away from the city.
sentences.n: ἐν δέ is ‘and in (it)’, most naturally the house, and πέλεν is the unaugmented imperfect of πέλω ‘be’. Σικελή is ‘Sicel’, a woman from the Sicels, and γρηῢς ‘old woman’ (Attic γραῦς). ἥ ῥα is ‘who’, with ῥα the particle of lively narration. γέροντα is ‘the old man’, Laertes. ἐνδυκέως is ‘kindly’, and κομέεσκεν is the iterative imperfect of κομέω ‘tend’. ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ is ‘on the farm’, and νόσφι πόληος ‘apart from the city’, πόληος being the genitive of πόλις.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ Ὀδυσεὺς δμώεσσι καὶ υἱέϊ μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: enth’ Odyseus dmōessi kai huieï mython eeipen·
sentences.l: There Odysseus to the servants and to his son a speech spoke:
sentences.i: There Odysseus spoke to the servants and to his son:
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘there’. δμώεσσι is the dative plural of δμώς ‘servant’, and υἱέϊ the dative of υἱός ‘son’. μῦθον ἔειπεν is ‘spoke a speech’, ἔειπεν being an epic aorist of λέγω. The line introduces a speech that begins in the next part, so no quotation mark is opened here.
